subtopic_detail: Adult requesting assessment for lifelong inattention with no documented childhood history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a twenty seven year old software tester who has booked a long appointment to discuss attention problems. He describes losing track of tasks, missing deadlines and needing to reread paragraphs since he can remember, and says a colleague on stimulant medication told him the description sounded familiar.

He completed an online self rating scale which scored in the likely range and he has brought the printout. He drinks alcohol on weekends only, uses no other substances, sleeps about seven hours and has never been treated for a mental illness. He mentions that he has a long commute and asks whether medication would let him drive more safely.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed and cooperative, speech normal in rate and form, mood described as frustrated with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Online self rating scale scores in the likely range, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him for formal neuropsychological testing, using the profile of results obtained on those tests to establish or exclude the diagnosis
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing describes cognitive strengths and weaknesses but neither confirms nor excludes the condition, since many people with the disorder perform normally in a quiet one to one setting. It is useful when a learning disorder is suspected alongside. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

options.text: Accept the self rating scale as sufficient evidence, make the diagnosis today and refer him to a psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy and skills training
options.rationale: Rating scales have poor specificity in adults because anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and substance use all generate similar scores. Making the diagnosis on a screening instrument risks both mislabelling and missing the treatable condition actually present. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD assessment)
source_refs: RACGP: Adult ADHD assessment

options.text: Treat the presentation as an anxiety disorder with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in six weeks before considering any further assessment
options.rationale: There is no described anxiety syndrome here, and empirical antidepressant treatment would delay assessment while attributing symptoms to a disorder he has not been shown to have. Comorbid anxiety is common but is identified rather than assumed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance

options.text: Seek collateral evidence of symptoms present in childhood, such as school reports and a family informant, before referring him for diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: Diagnosis requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of twelve and to have caused impairment in more than one setting, so retrospective corroboration is a core part of the assessment rather than an optional extra. Adult recall alone is unreliable and self rating scales are screening tools. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start a trial of immediate release methylphenidate and review the response after two weeks, using improvement in concentration to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Stimulants improve attention in people without the disorder, so a symptomatic response has no diagnostic value. Prescribing is also restricted in Australian jurisdictions to authorised prescribers under state stimulant regulations. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a valid and treatable diagnosis, but it is defined by symptoms beginning in childhood, so establishing the developmental history is central to assessment rather than a formality. Australian guidance expects several inattentive or hyperactive impulsive symptoms to have been present before the age of twelve, impairment in at least two settings, and exclusion of other explanations including sleep disorder, substance use, mood and anxiety disorders and thyroid disease. Self rating scales such as the adult self report scale are screening instruments with limited specificity, and neuropsychological testing cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis. Collateral information from school reports, parents or a long standing partner materially changes diagnostic accuracy and is the step most often skipped. Stimulant prescribing is regulated at state level in Australia, generally requiring an authorised prescriber, and driving advice depends on whether symptoms or treatment affect safe vehicle control rather than on the diagnostic label alone.
key_points: Symptoms must date from before the age of twelve and impair function in two or more settings.
Collateral history and school reports materially improve diagnostic accuracy.
Self rating scales screen rather than diagnose, with poor specificity in adults.
Neuropsychological testing cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
Stimulant prescribing in Australia is restricted to authorised prescribers under state regulation.
explanation.pearls: Screen deliberately for obstructive sleep apnoea and for stimulant misuse before referral, because untreated sleep fragmentation reproduces the entire inattentive symptom set, and a request framed around a specific drug or a colleague's prescription warrants the same careful history as any other controlled drug request.

sources.label: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Psychosis persisting for several weeks after the mood episode has resolved
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a twenty three year old woman on the inpatient unit six weeks after admission. She came in elated, sleeping two hours a night, spending beyond her means and convinced that she had been chosen to reform the banking system.

Her mood and sleep settled over the first fortnight with treatment and she now describes her mood as normal, is sleeping eight hours and has no pressure of speech. For the past four weeks, with a euthymic mood throughout, she has continued to believe that bank staff communicate about her in coded language and she still hears two voices commenting on her actions. She has had similar admissions twice before, and between them she has worked and lived independently. Urine drug screening has been negative on each admission.

data_table.Examination: Calm and cooperative, speech normal in rate and volume, mood euthymic with congruent affect, persistent referential delusions and third person auditory hallucinations, no thought disorder, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count, electrolytes, liver and thyroid function within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, given the sustained and well systematised belief about bank staff that has continued unchanged since the mood symptoms settled
options.rationale: This diagnosis requires the absence of prominent hallucinations and excludes people who have had full manic episodes, and she has both. Functioning outside the delusional theme is also typically preserved, which does not describe her admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Bipolar affective disorder, current episode in remission, with mood congruent psychotic features that are resolving more slowly than the mood symptoms
options.rationale: Psychotic symptoms in this disorder occur only during mood episodes, so several weeks of active psychosis with a euthymic mood does not fit. The content described is also referential and third person rather than grandiose and mood congruent. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, given psychosis persisting for weeks in the absence of mood symptoms alongside prominent mood episodes over the course of the illness
options.rationale: The defining feature is a period of two weeks or more of delusions or hallucinations without prominent mood symptoms, in an illness where mood episodes occupy the majority of the total duration. That pattern is exactly what has emerged over the past four weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms arising in reaction to the psychotic experiences and to the disruption caused by repeated hospital admissions
options.rationale: Full manic episodes with reduced sleep, overspending and grandiosity are not secondary demoralisation, and her interepisode functioning has been preserved. Prominent mood episodes occupying much of the illness argue against this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder, since stimulant use commonly produces both elevated mood and persistent referential beliefs in young adults of this age
options.rationale: Drug screening has been negative across three separate admissions and the symptoms have persisted far beyond any plausible period of intoxication or withdrawal. Screening cannot exclude every agent, but the longitudinal pattern is against it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between bipolar disorder with psychotic features and schizophrenia, and it is defined longitudinally rather than cross sectionally. The two requirements are a period of at least two weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, and mood episodes that are present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. If psychosis occurs only within mood episodes, the diagnosis is a mood disorder with psychotic features, while if mood episodes are brief and peripheral to a chronic psychotic illness, the diagnosis is schizophrenia. The distinction matters because it shapes maintenance treatment, with mood stabilisation and antipsychotic therapy usually both required, and because the prognosis lies between those of the two neighbouring diagnoses. Diagnosis often becomes clear only after the mood episode has been treated and the clinician looks at what remains, which is why the longitudinal course must be revisited rather than fixed at admission.
key_points: Two weeks or more of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms is the defining criterion.
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total illness duration.
Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features.
Brief peripheral mood symptoms in chronic psychosis indicate schizophrenia.
The diagnosis is longitudinal and is often clarified after the mood episode resolves.
explanation.pearls: Chart the timeline of mood symptoms against psychotic symptoms on paper with the patient and family, because the diagnosis turns entirely on which symptoms were present when, and reconstructing that sequence from memory in a clinic interview is the commonest reason these three diagnoses are confused.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Return to driving three weeks after a first episode of psychosis while still symptomatic
stem:
You are the doctor in the early psychosis service reviewing a twenty year old apprentice three weeks after discharge from his first admission with a psychotic episode. He was admitted with persecutory beliefs about being followed and has been taking risperidone since.

He tells you he has started driving himself to work again because his mother cannot keep taking time off. He still believes he is being followed by a particular car and describes checking his mirrors constantly, and he reports feeling sedated in the mornings. He holds an unconditional private vehicle licence and has had no accidents. He asks whether the medication will stop him driving.

data_table.Examination: Alert but slowed, speech normal in rate, mood flat with reactive affect, persecutory delusion held with moderate conviction, no hallucinations reported today, mild bradykinesia, no akathisia
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, fasting glucose and lipids within normal limits, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 412 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about driving?

options.text: Advise him that he should not drive at present, document the discussion and explain how the fitness to drive assessment and reporting obligations work
options.rationale: Active persecutory beliefs that direct his attention to other vehicles, together with sedation from recent treatment, mean he does not currently meet the medical criteria for an unconditional licence. Explaining the process honestly preserves the therapeutic relationship and supports later return to driving. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

options.text: Advise that driving is acceptable for a private vehicle provided he avoids night driving and long trips, and review the question again at his next appointment
options.rationale: The standards for private vehicles are less stringent than for commercial ones but still require that the condition does not impair the ability to drive safely. Restricting the hours of driving does not address a persecutory belief centred on another vehicle. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

options.text: Notify the driver licensing authority immediately without discussing it with him, since the risk to other road users overrides the usual duty of confidentiality
options.rationale: The ordinary course is to advise the patient of the obligation to report and to document that advice, with direct notification reserved for continued unsafe driving despite counselling, and even then the patient is normally informed. Bypassing the conversation damages engagement in a service he needs. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose to remove the morning sedation and tell him he may continue driving once he feels alert at the wheel in the mornings
options.rationale: Sedation is only part of the problem and the persistent delusional belief remains, so dose adjustment alone does not restore fitness. Using his subjective alertness as the test devolves a medical judgement to a symptom he cannot assess objectively. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

options.text: Tell him that a diagnosis of psychosis permanently disqualifies him from holding a driver licence and refer him for assistance with alternative transport arrangements
options.rationale: The standards are functional rather than diagnostic, and most people whose symptoms remit and who remain adherent return to driving, often on a conditional licence with periodic review. A permanent disqualification misstates the guidance and removes any incentive to disclose symptoms. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

explanation.summary: Australian fitness to drive standards are functional, asking whether the condition or its treatment impairs the ability to drive safely rather than turning on the diagnostic label. For psychotic illness the relevant features are active symptoms that could affect judgement or attention, such as persecutory beliefs involving traffic or vehicles, command hallucinations, and sedation or extrapyramidal effects from medication. The treating doctor advises the patient about fitness and about their legal obligation to report a long term condition to the licensing authority, and documents that advice. A conditional licence with periodic medical review is the usual pathway back once symptoms remit and treatment is stable, and most people with a treated psychotic illness do drive. Direct notification by the doctor is a fallback for the patient who continues to drive unsafely despite advice, and jurisdictions differ in whether that reporting is mandatory or discretionary, with the Northern Territory and South Australia having stricter provisions than other states.
key_points: The standards assess function and safety rather than diagnosis.
Active symptoms involving vehicles and treatment related sedation both impair fitness.
The doctor advises, documents and explains the patient's duty to report.
A conditional licence with review is the usual route back to driving.
Direct notification is reserved for continued unsafe driving despite advice.
explanation.pearls: Commercial vehicle standards are substantially stricter than private ones, so an apprentice who later moves into a driving role or acquires a heavy vehicle licence needs reassessment against the commercial criteria rather than carrying his private conditional licence across.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Purging several times weekly at normal body weight with dental erosion in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a twenty year old university student who discloses that she has been making herself vomit after eating for the past two years. It happens three or four times a week after episodes in which she eats far more than she intends and feels unable to stop.

She describes intense shame, weighs herself several times daily and judges herself almost entirely on her shape. Her weight is stable in the healthy range and her periods are regular. Her dentist has commented on erosion of the back of her front teeth. She has not tried any treatment before and is worried about what she should do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, erosion of the palatal surfaces of the upper incisors, mild parotid enlargement, no callus on the knuckles, no lanugo hair, no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-32), magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 408 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and start lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily, with dental review and monitoring of electrolytes
options.rationale: Lisdexamfetamine is registered for binge eating disorder, which does not involve compensatory purging, and stimulants can worsen restriction and weight preoccupation in this setting. The compensatory behaviour is what separates the two diagnoses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange dietitian review with self help materials alone and defer any psychological or pharmacological treatment until three months of monitoring have passed
options.rationale: Guided self help has a role as a first step in some services but withholding definitive treatment for months in an established two year illness allows the behaviour to entrench further. Dietetic input supports treatment rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and start fluoxetine 60 mg daily, with dental review and monitoring of electrolytes
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy targeting the binge and purge cycle is first line, and fluoxetine at this dose is the only antidepressant with established efficacy in reducing binge frequency in this disorder. The higher dose is specific to this indication rather than the usual antidepressant dose. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and start sertraline 50 mg daily, with dental review and monitoring of electrolytes
options.rationale: Other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not have the evidence base that exists for fluoxetine in this disorder, and a standard antidepressant dose has not been shown to reduce binge frequency. Choosing an alternative agent forfeits the one pharmacological option with good trial support. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Refer for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and start bupropion 150 mg daily, with dental review and monitoring of electrolytes
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in people who purge because of a markedly increased seizure risk in this population. That contraindication is absolute regardless of how attractive the drug's other properties appear. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviours and self evaluation dominated by shape and weight, and unlike anorexia nervosa the weight is usually in the healthy range, which is why the diagnosis is frequently missed for years. Physical clues include erosion of the palatal tooth surfaces, parotid enlargement, calluses on the knuckles and a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, and electrolyte disturbance is the main acute medical risk. Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the first line treatment and is available in Australia under an eating disorder treatment plan that funds a substantial number of psychological and dietetic sessions each year. Fluoxetine at sixty milligrams daily is the only medication with a clear evidence base, reducing binge and purge frequency, and the dose required is higher than the usual antidepressant dose. Dental review matters because erosion is irreversible, and patients are advised to rinse with water rather than brushing immediately after vomiting.
key_points: Weight is typically in the healthy range, so the diagnosis rests on behaviour and cognitions.
Vomiting produces hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis and irreversible dental erosion.
Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is first line treatment.
Fluoxetine at sixty milligrams daily is the only well supported medication.
Bupropion is contraindicated because of seizure risk in people who purge.
explanation.pearls: Advise rinsing with water or a fluoride mouthwash rather than brushing after vomiting, because brushing enamel that has just been bathed in gastric acid accelerates the erosion, and arrange an eating disorder treatment plan to fund the sessions rather than a standard mental health plan, which provides too few.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

subtopic_detail: Escalating online gambling losses with borrowing and concealment over twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a forty two year old plumber who has come in at his wife's insistence. Over the past year he has been betting on sport through a phone application, first with small amounts and then with progressively larger ones to recover losses.

He has taken out a personal loan she did not know about and has been paying the minimum on two credit cards. He describes restlessness when he tries to stop, and he has lied about where the money went. He sleeps poorly and says he feels hopeless when he thinks about the debt, though he denies any intention to harm himself when you ask directly. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and uses no other drugs.

data_table.Examination: Tired and tense with restless hands, speech normal in rate, mood low with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no evidence of intoxication or withdrawal, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer him to a financial counsellor to consolidate the debts and review him in three months, on the basis that resolving the debt will settle the behaviour
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable component but relieving debt without treating the disorder commonly funds further gambling. The behaviour is not a rational response to money problems and does not resolve when they do. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for the low mood and poor sleep, and review the gambling behaviour once his depressive symptoms have improved
options.rationale: Antidepressants have not been shown to reduce gambling behaviour, and mood symptoms here are closely tied to the losses and concealment. Treating them in isolation leaves the driver of the distress untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance

options.text: Advise him to install blocking software and set deposit limits on his accounts, and review him in six weeks to see whether the behaviour has settled
options.rationale: Access limiting measures help but are readily circumvented and are insufficient alone for a disorder of this severity with borrowing and concealment. Offering only self management also misses the elevated suicide risk. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling and assess his suicide risk formally, arranging financial counselling and self exclusion support
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy has the strongest evidence in this disorder, and formal risk assessment is essential because gambling disorder carries one of the highest suicide rates of any addictive disorder, driven by debt and shame. Financial counselling and self exclusion address the immediate access and harm. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Start naltrexone to reduce the urge to gamble and review him in four weeks, referring for psychological therapy only if the medication proves insufficient
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence as an adjunct, particularly with strong urges or comorbid alcohol problems, but they are not first line and do not address the cognitive distortions that drive the chasing of losses. Deferring therapy delays the intervention that works best. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance related and addictive disorders and shows the same features of tolerance, withdrawal like restlessness, loss of control, chasing losses, concealment and continued use despite harm. Australia has the highest per capita gambling losses in the world and online sports betting has changed the demographic profile toward younger working men, with the phone providing continuous access. Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the cognitive distortions of gambling, particularly the illusion of control and the belief that losses can be recovered, is the treatment with the best evidence, and free services are available nationally through the gambling help line and state services. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, with naltrexone the best studied agent for strong urges, particularly where alcohol problems coexist. Formal suicide risk assessment is mandatory at every review because the suicide rate in this disorder is among the highest in psychiatry, and the acute risk period often follows disclosure of debt to family.
key_points: The disorder is classified with addictive disorders and shows tolerance and loss of control.
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling specific cognitions is first line.
Naltrexone is an adjunct for strong urges rather than a first line treatment.
Financial counselling and self exclusion address access and harm but do not treat the disorder.
Suicide risk is high and must be assessed formally and repeatedly.
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about gambling in anyone presenting with unexplained debt, relationship breakdown or new low mood in a working age man, because patients almost never volunteer it, and screen the partner for distress too since family members of people with this disorder have markedly raised rates of depression and anxiety.

sources.label: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

subtopic_detail: Obsessive compulsive symptoms unchanged after six weeks on a low dose serotonergic antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a twenty nine year old teacher six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for obsessive compulsive disorder. She has intrusive thoughts about contamination and washes her hands until they crack, spending about three hours a day on rituals.

She has taken the tablet every day without missing a dose and reports no adverse effects beyond mild nausea in the first week. She has been on a waiting list for psychological therapy since the last visit and has not yet been seen. She estimates that nothing has changed and asks whether the medication is the wrong one for her.

data_table.Examination: Cracked and erythematous skin over both hands, mood mildly low with reactive affect, obsessions and compulsions described with good insight, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a regular benzodiazepine to relieve the distress associated with the intrusive thoughts and review her when a therapy appointment becomes available
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat this disorder and regular use undermines exposure therapy by suppressing the anxiety that the treatment depends on the patient tolerating. Dependence in a young adult with a chronic disorder is a predictable harm. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and continue for at least twelve weeks at the higher dose before judging whether this medication has failed her
options.rationale: This disorder responds to higher doses and over a longer period than depression, so six weeks at a starting dose is an incomplete trial rather than a failure. Escalating within the licensed range and waiting the full interval is what the evidence supports. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Switch to a different selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a starting dose and review the response after a further six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Switching before the first agent has had an adequate dose and duration simply restarts the clock and risks cycling through several drugs at subtherapeutic doses. Switching is reasonable only after a genuinely adequate trial. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Add a low dose antipsychotic as an augmenting agent now and continue the current sertraline dose, reviewing the combination after a further six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for people who remain symptomatic after an adequate trial of a serotonergic antidepressant at a high dose, usually with therapy as well. Using it early adds metabolic and movement risk without exhausting simpler options. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Stop the sertraline and rely on exposure and response prevention alone once a place becomes available, reviewing her again when therapy has commenced
options.rationale: Therapy is the treatment of choice and works well, but stopping an incompletely trialled medication while she waits leaves her without any active treatment at three hours of rituals a day. The two treatments are complementary rather than alternatives. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

explanation.summary: Obsessive compulsive disorder differs from depression in both the dose and the duration of antidepressant treatment required, and this is the single commonest reason treatment is wrongly declared to have failed. Higher doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are typically needed, often at the upper end of the licensed range, and response builds over ten to twelve weeks rather than the four to six weeks expected in depression. Exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment of choice and is at least as effective as medication, with the combination preferred for moderate to severe illness. When a genuinely adequate trial of one agent fails, options include switching to another serotonergic antidepressant, moving to clomipramine, or augmenting with a low dose antipsychotic such as aripiprazole or risperidone. Benzodiazepines have no role, both because they do not treat the disorder and because they blunt the anxiety that exposure therapy requires the patient to experience and tolerate.
key_points: Higher antidepressant doses are needed than for depression.
Allow ten to twelve weeks at an adequate dose before judging response.
Exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment of choice.
Antipsychotic augmentation follows an adequate failed trial rather than preceding it.
Benzodiazepines do not treat the disorder and interfere with exposure therapy.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about mental compulsions such as silent counting, praying or reviewing, because patients who deny rituals often perform them entirely in their heads, and therapy that targets only the visible handwashing leaves the covert compulsions maintaining the disorder.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders
